Before the startup of the limited aeration HA reactors, an oxygenation experiment in clean water was carried out to investigate the oxygen transfer characteristics of the bubble and bubbleless aeration. The essence of aeration is the gas-liquid mass transfer process. This process is generally described by double-film theory. Based -on this theory, the overall oxygen transfer coefficient kLa was used to evaluate the oxygen transfer performance as shown in Eqs. (1) (Mei et al., 2019). kLa was measured by the dynamic method according to the previous lectures (Garcia-Ochoa et al., 2009; Berth et al., 2019). The specific operation process was as follows: firstly, in the absence of aeration, oxygen was removed from the clean water with flushing nitrogen, thus controlling the initial level of DO. Secondly, air was turned back on and the change in the DO concentration was monitored with the DO online monitoring probe. When the DO concentration was stabilized (t=t1), the DO in the system was continuously monitored for the sufficient data to be collected (t=t2). The variations of DO were measured under different aeration pressures (0.010 MPa, 0.030 MPa, and 0.050 MPa) and at different circulation ratios (10, 20, and 30). During the experiment, the water temperature in the reactors was maintained at 25°C using the automatic temperature control system.
where KLa is the overall oxygen transfer coefficient, h-1; C* is the saturated dissolved oxygen concentration in water (25°C, 8.34 mg/L); C is the dissolved oxygen in water at t (h), mg/L.

Text S3 Label-free quantitative proteomic profiling

Four samples (MBL-MHA-I, MBL-MHA-II, MHA and HA) were all 100 mL each, centrifuged for 15 min at 8000 rpm, respectively, then the supernatants were discarded and the precipitates were reserved and stored at −80 °C until analysis (three parallel samples were set for each sample). Proteins were extracted from three samples and the protein concentrations were measured using the BCA kit (Thermo Scientific Pierce) with standard curve. Then the protein samples were subjected to SDS-PAGE electrophoresis. The purified proteins were reduced and alkylated according to the manufacturer’s instructions of protein alkylated Kit (Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA) with some modifications. The alkylated protein samples were digested overnight at 37 °C with trypsin and Sep-Pak was used to remove added salts, detergents, and other interfering substances. The desalted peptides were quantified according to the manufacturer’s instructions of peptide quantitative Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, No.23275, USA). 0.5 g/μL peptides were dissolved with mass spectrometric buffer solution and the analyses were performed using a Q-Exactive Plus Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). MS analysis was performed in three biological triplicates for each sample to ensure the accuracy of the mass spectrometry results. The raw mass spectrometry MS/MS spectra search was processed using PEAKS Studio 8.5. The protein quantification and calculation of statistical significance were carried out using Student’s t-test and error correction (p-value < 0.05) using the method of Benjamini–Hochberg. To perform functional analysis, the identified proteins were carried on the follow-up biological information function analysis using GO (Gene Ontology, http://www.geneontology.org/). Pathway mapping of identified proteins was performed using the KEGG database (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, http://www.genome.jp/kegg/) (Poleti et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2018).
